note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. Chapters 2-19 are authored here. Chapter 1 is deliberately absent: its lessons are still schema_version 1 with no practises.knowledge, so no payoff can be claimed for it honestly, and it owns no core/book-generation.json target either. Chapters 2-5 have a terminal practice-mix; chapters 6-19 have none, so their payoff is the chapter's last lesson by sequence, which is where the recombination and wrap-up recall actually live. Chapter 2 carries two practice-mix lessons; the terminal one, PT-C02-formal-practice, is the payoff.

chapters.title: How Are You?
chapters.label: ch:pt-how-are-you
chapters.canDo: I can ask a Portuguese speaker how they are, casually or respectfully, and answer for myself.

payoff.summary: The full Chapter 2 exchange: greet, ask Tudo bem?, answer for yourself, and hand the question back. PT-C02-formal-practice then rebuilds the same exchange for respect (Como está o senhor?), so the chapter's canDo covers both registers.

chapters.title: Introducing Yourself
chapters.label: ch:pt-introductions
chapters.canDo: I can give my name in Portuguese, ask for someone else's, and say that it is a pleasure.

payoff.summary: A whole first meeting: Olá, me chamo …, Como se chama?, prazer — then the same exchange again with o senhor and a senhora.

chapters.title: Farewells
chapters.label: ch:pt-farewells
chapters.canDo: I can close a Portuguese conversation and pick the goodbye that matches when I will next see the person.

payoff.summary: Open with Olá, ask Tudo bem?, then choose the exit — até logo, até amanhã, até breve, or adeus, to God, for the one that means for good.

chapters.title: The First Verbs
chapters.label: ch:pt-first-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can build my own Portuguese sentences with -ar verbs and say what I speak, where I live and where I work.

payoff.summary: Conjugate falar, morar and trabalhar across eu, tu and você with the pronoun dropped, then answer Você fala português? and Onde você mora? about yourself.

chapters.title: Numbers One to Ten
chapters.label: ch:pt-numbers-one-to-ten
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to ten in Portuguese and hear the old numbers still sitting inside setembro and dezembro.

payoff.summary: Count um to dez, pair sete, oito, nove and dez with setembro, outubro, novembro and dezembro, and hear Latin's -ct- become the -it- of oito, noite and leite.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:pt-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name all seven Portuguese days and count the weekdays from domingo the way Portuguese does.

payoff.summary: Run domingo, segunda, terça, quarta, quinta, sexta, sábado, and explain why Monday is the second day: domingo, the Lord's day, is counted first.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:pt-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can tell the time in Portuguese and use meio-dia and meia-noite for the two hours that take no number.

payoff.summary: Say meio-dia and meia-noite, split each into meio or meia plus dia or noite, and catch noctem → noite as the same shift that gave oito.

chapters.title: Months and Seasons
chapters.label: ch:pt-months-and-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name the Portuguese months and seasons and explain how verão grew out of a word for spring.

payoff.summary: Give a primavera, o verão, o outono, o inverno, then trace verão back through vērānum to vēr, spring — the summer word grown out of the spring one.

chapters.title: Family
chapters.label: ch:pt-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my parents and my siblings in Portuguese and say why irmão is not built on Latin's frater.

payoff.summary: Say o pai, a mãe, o irmão, a irmã with their nasal endings, then cut frāter germānus down to germānus alone and land on irmão, twin of Spanish hermano.

chapters.title: Bread, Water, and Wine
chapters.label: ch:pt-bread-water-wine
chapters.canDo: I can name bread, water and wine in Portuguese and hear the -nh- of vinho as Spanish's ñ.

payoff.summary: Say o pão, a água and o vinho, hold água against French's worn-down eau, and pronounce the palatal -nh- of vinho, already met in amanhã.

chapters.title: Numbers Eleven to Twenty
chapters.label: ch:pt-numbers-eleven-to-twenty
chapters.canDo: I can count from eleven to twenty in Portuguese and read dezesseis as the little sentence ten-and-six that it is.

payoff.summary: Run onze to vinte, hear dez e seis inside dezesseis, and note that Portuguese breaks from the fused teens at 16, a number earlier than French or Italian.

chapters.title: Colours
chapters.label: ch:pt-colours
chapters.canDo: I can name black, white, red and blue in Portuguese and say why not one of the four is a plain inherited Latin colour word.

payoff.summary: Say preto, branco, vermelho and azul, take vermelho back to vermiculus, the little worm crushed for dye, and azul back to Arabic lāzaward.

chapters.title: Having and Telling Your Age
chapters.label: ch:pt-having-and-age
chapters.canDo: I can ask a Portuguese speaker's age and give my own, holding my years with ter rather than being them.

payoff.summary: Ask Quantos anos tens?, answer Tenho vinte anos — literally I hold twenty years — and set Portuguese's simplified ano against Spanish's palatalised año.

chapters.title: The Past Portuguese Kept
chapters.label: ch:pt-past-portuguese-kept
chapters.canDo: I can say in Portuguese what I did with the simple past, and avoid reading tenho falado as I have spoken.

payoff.summary: Put falei com ele ontem, one finished act, beside tenho falado com ele, repeatedly and lately, and say out loud why the compound never took the simple past's job.

chapters.title: Ser and Estar
chapters.label: ch:pt-ser-and-estar
chapters.canDo: I can choose between ser and estar in Portuguese and change what an adjective means by switching them.

payoff.summary: Say Ela é bonita and Ela está bonita back to back, then A sopa é boa and a sopa está boa, naming the quality against the current condition each time.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:pt-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can name the head and the hand in Portuguese and explain the nasal vowel that swallowed the n of manus.

payoff.summary: Say a cabeça and a mão, pluralise to as mãos, and follow the n of manus dissolving between vowels, as it did in lua, boa and pão.

chapters.title: Verbs at the Core
chapters.label: ch:pt-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say I am, I have, I go, I come, I say, I see and I know in Portuguese, pick the right member of its two be-verbs and its two know-verbs, and name the English words each verb left behind.

payoff.summary: The chapter's last lesson closes the set: after saber and conhecer the reader produces all nine first-person forms in one run - sou, estou, tenho, vou, venho, digo, vejo, sei, conheco - and re-derives the roots behind estar and ter.

chapters.title: More Verbs at the Core
chapters.label: ch:pt-more-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can say that I think, understand, read, write, take, ask, help and like in Portuguese, choose between its two verbs for taking and its two for understanding, and keep de attached to gostar.

payoff.summary: The chapter's last lesson closes the set: after gostar de the reader produces all eight first-person forms in one run - penso, entendo, leio, escrevo, pego, pergunto, ajudo, gosto - explains why the de cannot be dropped, and ties gostar back to saber as the second Portuguese verb that stopped meaning to taste.
